deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivation. It is the second sheet of a heavily corrected draft of an official expert opinion (Gutachten), apparently addressed to the Hanoverian government. It concerns Generalleutnant J. J. Baeyer's proposal (his 1861 pamphlet 'Über die Größe und Figur der Erde') to join the central-European triangulations into one arc. This proposal led to the Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung of 1862.

The content runs as follows.

(1) Baeyer proposed reconciling neighbouring triangulation chains: compute the common sides from both networks and split the discrepancy by weights (described on the previous page). Riemann's draft says that if these proposals are generally and definitively adopted, Hannover could take on the new determinations required for its own triangle system, provided it is given the necessary means. In several struck and rewritten versions he adds a reservation. Unconditional acceptance faces objections, because adjusting the chains against each other piecemeal is not optimal, and 'something more perfect can easily be achieved by another route.' This is an implicit preference for a joint least-squares adjustment of the whole network, but nothing is worked out.

(2) On the astronomical part: what limits the use of geodetic measurements for the figure of the Earth is precisely the lack of sufficiently exact astronomical longitudes and latitudes. For this reason even the Hanoverian (Gauss) arc, which rests on a common base, could not be used over its whole length. Only the stretch Göttingen–Altona was usable, together with the Danish stretch Altona/Lauenburg–(probably) Lysabbel. Hannover could contribute useful material by determining longitude (and latitude) differences between Göttingen and other observatories. With modern means this would be far cheaper. For longitudes by telegraph, connecting the Göttingen observatory to the telegraph network would be a necessary precondition.

(3) Start of a conceptual section 'zur schärferen Bestimmung der Gestalt der Erde', with these definitions:
- The 'mathematical surface of the Earth' is the level surface (Niveaufläche) coinciding with the surface of the resting sea, i.e. the geoid. It deviates from a rotation ellipsoid only by small wave-like elevations and depressions.
- The direction of the normal to the level surface (the plumb line) determines astronomical latitude and longitude (Φ, Λ).
- The normal to the ellipsoid determines geodetic latitude and longitude (φ, λ).
- The angle between plumb line and ellipsoid normal is called the local deflection of the vertical (Lotabweichung). In modern notation (mine, not on the page) its components are ξ = Φ − φ and η = (Λ − λ) cos φ.

No computations appear.

results.what: Definition of the geoid as the equipotential surface of the resting sea, deviating slightly and wave-like from a rotation ellipsoid; astronomical vs. geodetic coordinates; local deflection of the vertical as the angle between plumb line and ellipsoid normal.
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (1828, Bestimmung des Breitenunterschiedes zwischen Göttingen und Altona), Bessel; term 'Geoid' by J. B. Listing (1873)

results.what: Methodological remark that Baeyer's pairwise splitting of side discrepancies between triangulation chains is inferior to a more perfect (implicitly joint least-squares) adjustment.
results.modern_name: Network adjustment by least squares (vs. piecewise chain adjustment)

results.what: Recommendation of telegraphic longitude determination between Göttingen and other observatories, requiring connection of the Göttingen observatory to the telegraph network.
results.usually_credited_to: US Coast Survey (1840s), widely used in Europe in the 1850s–60s

deep.surprise_reason: This is an administrative/scientific advisory draft on Baeyer's Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung with standard geodetic definitions (geoid, deflection of the vertical). It contains no mathematics. Riemann's involvement as a Göttingen expert is historically interesting but contains nothing technically new for 1861/62.

checkable.sympy: Phi, phi, Lam, lam = symbols('Phi phi Lam lam'); xi = Phi - phi; eta = (Lam - lam)*cos(phi); simplify(sqrt(xi**2+eta**2).subs({Phi:phi, Lam:lam}))
checkable.asserts: My modern addition, not on the page: the total deflection of the vertical vanishes when astronomical and geodetic coordinates coincide (result 0).

transcription_corrections: 'als unvergeßlich[?] bezeichnet' is more likely 'als unumgänglich bezeichnet' (or similar).
'... Karte[?]:' at the end of line 4 is uncertain; context suggests a phrase like 'gern übernehmen' (Hannover would undertake the new determinations), not 'Karte'.

In the Gradmessung sentence, the struck words read roughly 'Theil und zwischen Altona-Lauenburg und Lysabbel'. The usable stretches meant are Göttingen–Altona (Gauss) and the Danish arc Lauenburg–Lysabbel (Schumacher); 'einerseits' is doubtful, as the image suggests 'Altona und Göttingen und [Theil] zwischen Altona-Lauenburg ...'.
'Aufwande an Zeit[?] Mühe und Kosten': the image supports 'Aufwande an Zeit, Mühe und Kosten' or just 'Mühe und Kosten'.
Before 'Telegraphie', the interlinear insertion reads approximately 'für die Bestimmung der Längen mit Hülfe der Telegraphie würde jedoch ...'.
The last word may be 'Localablenkung' rather than 'Localabweichung' of the Lothes; the reading is uncertain.
